analysis.one_liner: Cancels unspent IRS enforcement and taxpayer-service funding to fund tariff collection instead.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by one senator with zero cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in January 2025 and has had no hearing, vote, or other action since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill cancels every dollar of unspent IRS funding from the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act — money originally set aside for enforcing tax law, helping taxpayers, upgrading computer systems, and studying a free government tax-filing option. It then expresses Congress's opinion that the same amount should be spent on an 'External Revenue Service,' Senator Moreno's idea for an agency focused on collecting money from tariffs and foreign trade rather than from domestic taxpayers. The redirect is only a nonbinding statement; the actual effect of the bill is the funding cut.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses with unpaid or underreported taxes, since a smaller enforcement budget means fewer resources for auditing returns and collecting what is owed. The commercial tax-preparation industry also benefits, because the bill cancels funding for research into a free, direct government e-filing system that would compete with paid software.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners with unpaid taxes; tax-prep companies

how_it_helps.text: The bill rescinds all unobligated balances appropriated under section 10301 of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, which covered IRS enforcement, taxpayer services, operations support, business systems modernization, and a task force studying free direct e-filing. [S2] [S3]

It also rescinds unobligated funds for Treasury oversight offices including the Tax Inspector General, the Office of Tax Policy, the U.S. Tax Court, and other Treasury offices supporting the IRS. [S2]
For anyone with unpaid or underreported tax liability, a smaller enforcement budget means less auditing and collection activity directed at them. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary taxpayers who rely on IRS customer service, free e-filing research, and a tax system where people who owe actually pay; when enforcement shrinks, uncollected taxes pile up and the burden of funding the government shifts toward people who pay what they owe. Audits historically skew toward lower-income returns, particularly Earned Income Tax Credit claimants, when enforcement budgets tighten.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ordinary taxpayers and IRS customer service

drawbacks.text: The rescinded funds covered tax determination and collection enforcement, so the bill directly shrinks the IRS's ability to collect taxes that are legally owed. [S2]
The bill cancels funding for a task force researching a free, direct electronic tax-filing option, eliminating the only work toward a government-run alternative to paid filing software. [S2]

The 'External Revenue Service' redirect is a nonbinding sense of Congress — the bill rescinds the money but does not actually appropriate anything for a new agency, so the funds simply vanish from the budget rather than being redeployed. [S3]
Rescinding funds for the Tax Inspector General, Tax Court, and Treasury oversight offices cuts not just enforcement but the offices that police the IRS itself. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's one concrete effect is canceling unspent IRS funding from the 2022 law; its stated purpose of redirecting that money to a new tariff-focused agency is only an opinion statement with no appropriation attached. The cost falls on tax administration — enforcement, taxpayer services, modernization, and free-filing research — while the benefit goes to those who owe taxes they don't currently pay and to the paid tax-prep industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote since January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Moreno introduced the bill on January 21, 2025, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance. [S5]
No cosponsors have joined the bill. [S4]
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the action history after the January 21 referral. [S5]
Congress remains in session until January 2027, so the bill technically remains pending, but bills that sit in committee without a hearing rarely advance. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers are better off so far, because the IRS enforcement, taxpayer-service, and free-filing money the bill would cancel is still in place. No one has gained from the bill itself, which has not moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, taxpayers — the bill went nowhere

for.name: Sen. Bernie Moreno
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to rescind unspent IRS funding and called for redirecting it to an External Revenue Service.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving it stalled in committee. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: There have been no votes, and the bill has a single Republican sponsor with no cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: High-income households and businesses with unpaid or underreported taxes
industries.note: The bill cancels funding for tax determination and collection enforcement, shrinking the IRS's ability to audit returns and collect what is owed. What goes uncollected has to be made up by taxpayers who pay in full.
The bill rescinds funding for a task force researching a free, direct government e-filing system — the main government alternative to paid filing software. Cancelling it removes a competitive threat.

The bill states Congress's opinion that rescinded funds should go to an 'External Revenue Service' focused on collecting revenue from tariffs rather than domestic taxes. This is nonbinding and appropriates nothing, so its effect is symbolic.

analysis.trajectory: With no cosponsors, no hearing, and no committee action eight months after referral, the bill is very unlikely to advance in this Congress. Single-sponsor bills that sit through a Finance Committee session without a markup typically die quietly when the Congress ends.
